claim: Extinction of fear responses is critical for adaptive behavior.
source: Extinction of fear responses is critical for adaptive behavior and deficits in this form of safety learning are hallmark of anxiety disorders.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of fear extinction that is part of established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Deficits in fear extinction learning are hallmark of anxiety disorders.
source: Extinction of fear responses is critical for adaptive behavior and deficits in this form of safety learning are hallmark of anxiety disorders.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Dopamine neurons in the VTA are activated by the omission of the aversive unconditioned stimulus during fear extinction.
source: Here we show, using single-unit electrophysiology and cell-type specific fiber photometry, that dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) are activated by the omission of the aversive unconditioned stimulus (US) during fear extinction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-unit recordings and fiber photometry experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The dopamine signal occurs specifically during the beginning of extinction when the US omission is unexpected.
source: This dopamine signal occurred specifically during the beginning of extinction when the US omission is unexpected, and correlated strongly with extinction learning.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential responses during early vs. late extinction trials.

claim: The dopamine signal during US omission correlated strongly with extinction learning.
source: This dopamine signal occurred specifically during the beginning of extinction when the US omission is unexpected, and correlated strongly with extinction learning.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between calcium signals and behavioral extinction measures shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The dopamine signal during US omission is necessary for normal fear extinction learning.
source: Furthermore, temporally-specific optogenetic inhibition or excitation of dopamine neurons at the time of the US omission revealed that this dopamine signal is both necessary for, and sufficient to accelerate, normal fear extinction learning.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments showing impaired extinction when DA neurons are inhibited during US omission.

claim: Optogenetic excitation of dopamine neurons at the time of US omission is sufficient to accelerate fear extinction learning.
source: Furthermore, temporally-specific optogenetic inhibition or excitation of dopamine neurons at the time of the US omission revealed that this dopamine signal is both necessary for, and sufficient to accelerate, normal fear extinction learning.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic excitation experiments showing accelerated extinction when DA neurons are activated during US omission.

claim: Fear extinction represents new learning rather than forgetting or erasure of the original fear memory.
source: A large body of evidence indicates that fear extinction represents new learning rather than forgetting or the erasure of the original fear memory (Bouton et al., 2006; Myers and Davis, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The absence of the expected aversive outcome must be detected and signaled to brain regions mediating fear extinction in order to initiate extinction learning.
source: In order to initiate extinction learning, the absence of the expected aversive outcome must be detected and signaled to the brain regions mediating fear extinction.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on learning theory principles.

claim: A distributed network of brain structures including the amygdala, medial prefrontal cortex and hippocampus mediates the acquisition, consolidation and retrieval of fear extinction memories.
source: Decades of research on fear extinction has revealed that a distributed network of brain structures including the amygdala, medial prefrontal cortex and hippocampus mediates the acquisition, consolidation and retrieval of fear extinction memories (Duvarci and Pare, 2014; Maren et al., 2013; Pape and Pare, 2010; Sotres-Bayon and Quirk, 2010; Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: None of the brain structures in the fear extinction network have been shown to signal the absence of the expected aversive outcome during fear extinction.
source: However, none of these structures have been shown to signal the absence of the expected aversive outcome during fear extinction.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of evidence in the literature.

claim: New learning is initiated when outcomes violate expectations.
source: New learning is initiated when outcomes violate expectations (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972).
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of learning theory supported by citation.

claim: Violations of expectations cause 'prediction error' signals that initiate neural processes leading to changes in behavior.
source: Such violations are thought to cause 'prediction error' signals that initiate the neural processes which ultimately lead to changes in behavior (Friston, 2012; den Ouden et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: During fear extinction, the absence of the US is an unexpected event and likely generates a prediction error signal that initiates extinction learning.
source: During fear extinction, the absence of the US is an unexpected event and likely generates a prediction error signal that initiates extinction learning.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from learning theory principles.

claim: The omission of the aversive US can be conceptualized as a better-than-expected outcome.
source: More specifically, the omission of the aversive US can be conceptualized as a better-than-expected outcome.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation based on prediction error theory.

claim: The activity of midbrain dopamine neurons represents the degree to which outcomes are better or worse than expected.
source: It is well-established that the activity of midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons represents the degree to which outcomes are better or worse than expected (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Eshel et al., 2015; Eshel et al., 2016; Schultz et al., 1997; Schultz and Dickinson, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many DA neurons increase their firing to rewards that are either unexpected or better than expected.
source: For example, many DA neurons increase their firing to rewards that are either unexpected or better than expected and this DA signal is sufficient to drive reinforcement learning (Steinberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The DA signal in response to unexpected or better-than-expected rewards is sufficient to drive reinforcement learning.
source: For example, many DA neurons increase their firing to rewards that are either unexpected or better than expected and this DA signal is sufficient to drive reinforcement learning (Steinberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: An increase in DA release has been observed in the nucleus accumbens during fear extinction.
source: Consistent with this, an increase in DA release has been observed in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) during fear extinction (Badrinarayan et al., 2012) and pharmacological blockade of DA receptors in the NAc impairs fear extinction (Holtzman-Assif et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of DA receptors in the NAc impairs fear extinction.
source: Consistent with this, an increase in DA release has been observed in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) during fear extinction (Badrinarayan et al., 2012) and pharmacological blockade of DA receptors in the NAc impairs fear extinction (Holtzman-Assif et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The electrical activity of DA neurons during fear extinction, particularly at the time of the aversive US omission, and its relationship to extinction learning, is incompletely understood.
source: However, the electrical activity of DA neurons during fear extinction − particularly at the time of the aversive US omission − and its relationship to extinction learning, is incompletely understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A total of 43 out of 90 VTA neurons were classified as 'putative' DA neurons during day 1 recordings.
source: A total of 43 (out of 90) and 40 (out of 75) VTA neurons classified as 'putative' DA neurons (see Materials and methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 3) were recorded during day 1 and day 2, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: A total of 40 out of 75 VTA neurons were classified as 'putative' DA neurons during day 2 recordings.
source: A total of 43 (out of 90) and 40 (out of 75) VTA neurons classified as 'putative' DA neurons (see Materials and methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 3) were recorded during day 1 and day 2, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: 25% of putative DA neurons (10 of 40) exhibited a significant increase in firing rate to the omission of the aversive US during early extinction trials.
source: Analysis of neuronal firing rates during the time of the US omission revealed that 25% of putative DA neurons (10 of 40) exhibited a significant increase in firing rate to the omission of the aversive US during the early extinction trials (E-Ext: average of first 10 CSs) when the US omission was unexpected (Figure 1G-I;Figure 1—figure supplement 3B; see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data analysis.

claim: Only 2.3% of neurons (1 of 43) showed increased firing at the end of the CS during tone habituation.
source: This was not simply a response to the CS offset since only 2.3% of neurons (1 of 43; Figure 1H;Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) showed increased firing at the end of the CS during tone habituation (Hab).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data analysis.

claim: During late extinction trials, only 7.5% of putative DA neurons (3 of 40) showed an increase in firing to the absence of the US.
source: On the other hand, during late extinction trials (L-Ext: average of last 10 CSs), when the US omission was no longer unexpected and animals showed significant extinction of fear responses (Figure 1F), only 7.5% of putative DA neurons (3 of 40; Figure 1G-I) showed an increase in firing to the absence of the US.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no difference in freezing levels during the CS and the post-CS period in early extinction.
source: Importantly, there was no difference in freezing levels during the CS and the post-CS period in E-Ext (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) suggesting that the observed increase in DA neuron firing was not due to an increase in movement when the CS terminates.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The observed increase in DA neuron firing was not due to an increase in movement when the CS terminates.
source: Importantly, there was no difference in freezing levels during the CS and the post-CS period in E-Ext (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) suggesting that the observed increase in DA neuron firing was not due to an increase in movement when the CS terminates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data showing no difference in freezing.

claim: None of the putative DA neurons (0 of 40) showed a selective decrease in firing to the US omission during either early or late extinction.
source: Furthermore, analysis of the distribution of z-scores during the US omission (Figure 2A) revealed that none of the putative DA neurons (0 of 40) showed a selective decrease in firing to the US omission (see Materials and methods for details) during either E-Ext or L-Ext.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data analysis.

claim: The dominant response of putative DA neurons to US omission was excitatory.
source: This suggests that the dominant response of putative DA neurons to US omission was excitatory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of inhibited neurons and presence of excited neurons.

claim: There was a significant increase in firing to the US omission at the population level during early extinction but not late extinction or habituation.
source: Consistent with this, we observed a significant increase in firing to the US omission at the population level when we examined the average response of all putative DA neurons during E-Ext (paired t-test, t(39) = 2.22, p = 0.03), but not L-Ext (paired t-test, t(39) = 0.20, p = 0.83) or Hab (paired t-test, t(42) = 0.71, p = 0.47; Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of population-level electrophysiology data.

claim: 8.5% of putative non-DA neurons (3 of 35) showed a selective decrease in firing to the US omission during early extinction.
source: To test this possibility, we analyzed the activity of putative non-DA neurons – the subset of VTA neurons which likely dominantly includes GABA cells – during the time of the US omission and found that 8.5% of neurons (3 of 35) showed a selective decrease in firing to the US omission during E-Ext (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data analysis.

claim: The proportion of non-DA neurons showing decreased firing during US omission in early extinction was not significantly different from the proportion showing decreased firing at CS offset during habituation.
source: However, this was not significantly different from the proportion of non-DA neurons (4.2%, 2 of 47 neurons) showing decreased firing at the CS offset during Hab (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, Figure 2B; Fisher's exact test, p = 0.64).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The excitation observed in putative DA neurons during US omission is unlikely mediated by the activity of local GABA neurons.
source: These results therefore suggest that the excitation observed in the putative DA neurons during US omission is unlikely mediated by the activity of the local GABA neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of significant changes in non-DA neuron activity.

claim: Only 2.8% of putative non-DA neurons (1 of 35) showed increased firing at the time of the US omission during early extinction.
source: Moreover, only a small proportion of putative non-DA neurons showed increased firing at the time of the US omission during E-Ext (2.8%, 1 of 35 neurons; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data analysis.

claim: The US omission is signaled specifically by the putative DA neurons in VTA.
source: Together, these results suggest that the putative non-DA, likely local GABA, neurons in VTA do not change their firing at the time of the US omission and that the US omission is signaled specifically by the putative DA neurons in VTA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential responses of DA vs. non-DA neurons.

claim: The responses of putative DA neurons during the CS were diverse.
source: In contrast to the uniform response observed during US omission, the responses of putative DA neurons during the CS were diverse.
evidence: This is supported by examples shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: 5% of putative DA neurons (2 of 40) exhibited CS-evoked excitation during early extinction.
source: We found that 5% (2 of 40) of putative DA neurons exhibited CS-evoked excitation and 7.5% (3 of 40) CS-evoked inhibition during E-Ext.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data analysis.

claim: 7.5% of putative DA neurons (3 of 40) exhibited CS-evoked inhibition during early extinction.
source: We found that 5% (2 of 40) of putative DA neurons exhibited CS-evoked excitation and 7.5% (3 of 40) CS-evoked inhibition during E-Ext.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data analysis.

claim: The average activity of putative DA neurons in the VTA did not change during the CS.
source: These results suggest that the average activity of putative DA neurons in the VTA did not change during the CS even though different subsets of cells showed CS-evoked excitation and inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by population-level analysis showing no significant change.

claim: A lack of strong responses to the CS might be due to the cued fear conditioning paradigm used in the study.
source: A lack of strong responses to the CS might be due to the cued fear conditioning paradigm that we used in our study.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with other studies.

claim: DA neurons respond strongly to the CS when a discriminative fear conditioning task is used.
source: It has recently been shown that DA neurons respond strongly to the CS when a discriminative fear conditioning task is used and the strength of their response increases with increasing discrimination between the aversive and the safe CS (Jo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: There was a high degree of overlap between Cre-dependent gCaMP6 expression and immunohistochemical staining against tyrosine hydroxylase.
source: Accordingly, we observed a high degree of overlap between Cre-dependent gCaMP6 expression and immunohistochemical staining against tyrosine hydroxylase (TH; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Recordings from gCaMP6-expressing animals revealed transient increases in fluorescence whereas such increases were absent in mice expressing GFP.
source: Recordings from gCaMP6-expressing animals revealed transient increases in fluorescence whereas such increases were absent in mice expressing GFP (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by photometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Reward delivery caused large increases in fluorescence in the gCaMP6-expressing mice.
source: Furthermore, consistent with electrophysiological studies in VTA DA neurons (Eshel et al., 2015; Eshel et al., 2016; Roesch et al., 2007), we also confirmed that reward delivery caused large increases in fluorescence in the gCaMP6-expressing mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, also see Materials and methods), indicating that this Ca+2 signal is indeed generated by DA neuron activity.
evidence: This is supported by photometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Ca+2 signal measured by fiber photometry is generated by DA neuron activity.
source: Furthermore, consistent with electrophysiological studies in VTA DA neurons (Eshel et al., 2015; Eshel et al., 2016; Roesch et al., 2007), we also confirmed that reward delivery caused large increases in fluorescence in the gCaMP6-expressing mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, also see Materials and methods), indicating that this Ca+2 signal is indeed generated by DA neuron activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reward response data and consistency with previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: gCaMP6- and GFP-expressing animals showed comparable levels of freezing to the CS across sessions.
source: Both gCaMP6- and GFP-expressing animals underwent the same fear conditioning protocol as in the electrophysiology experiment (Figure 3D–E) and showed comparable levels of freezing to the CS across sessions (two-way repeated measures ANOVA; main effect of group: F1,24 = 0.04, p = 0.83; group × trial interaction: F2,24 = 0.04, p = 0.96; Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: During early extinction, there was a significant increase in the Ca+2 signal of gCaMP6 animals at the time of the US omission compared to the pre-CS baseline.
source: During E-Ext, we observed a significant increase in the Ca+2 signal of gCaMP6 animals at the time of the US omission compared to the pre-CS baseline (p<0.01, sign-rank test) and the GFP control group (p<0.01, rank-sum test; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of photometry data.

claim: During early extinction, the Ca+2 signal of gCaMP6 animals at the time of the US omission was significantly higher than the GFP control group.
source: During E-Ext, we observed a significant increase in the Ca+2 signal of gCaMP6 animals at the time of the US omission compared to the pre-CS baseline (p<0.01, sign-rank test) and the GFP control group (p<0.01, rank-sum test; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of photometry data.

claim: During late extinction, the Ca+2 signal did not change during the post-CS period.
source: On the other hand, during L-Ext, when the US omission was no longer unexpected, the Ca+2 signal did not change during the post-CS period (p = 0.85, sign-rank test; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of photometry data.

claim: No changes in fluorescence were observed in GFP-expressing animals during either early or late extinction.
source: No changes in fluorescence were observed in GFP-expressing animals during either E-Ext or L-Ext (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a direct report of photometry data.

claim: There was no change in the Ca+2 signal during habituation in the gCaMP6 group.
source: Furthermore, we did not observe any change in the Ca+2 signal during Hab (gCaMP6 group, p = 0.32, sign-rank test; Figure 3G) suggesting that the increase during US omission is unlikely a response to the CS offset.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of photometry data.

claim: The increase in Ca+2 signal during US omission is unlikely a response to the CS offset.
source: Furthermore, we did not observe any change in the Ca+2 signal during Hab (gCaMP6 group, p = 0.32, sign-rank test; Figure 3G) suggesting that the increase during US omission is unlikely a response to the CS offset.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of response during habituation.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the Ca+2 signal during early extinction and the change in freezing from early to late extinction.
source: This revealed a significant correlation between the Ca+2 signal during E-Ext and the change in freezing from E-Ext to L-Ext (Spearman's correlation = = 0.83, p = 0.0037; Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of photometry and behavioral data.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the Ca+2 signal during early extinction and the freezing levels during late extinction.
source: A significant correlation was also observed between the Ca+2 signal during E-Ext and the freezing levels during L-Ext (Spearman's correlation = 0.92, p = 0.0003).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of photometry and behavioral data.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the change in freezing from early to late extinction and reward responses.
source: We therefore examined the correlation between the change in freezing from E-Ext to L-Ext and reward responses and did not find a significant relationship between these two variables (Spearman's correlation = 0.32, p = 0.36; Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of photometry and behavioral data.

claim: The magnitude of the Ca+2 signal during early extinction correlated with the level of extinction learning.
source: These results therefore suggest that the magnitude of the Ca+2 signal during E-Ext correlated with the level of extinction learning and the variations in the magnitude of this signal were not due to differences in the recording location.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analyses showing relationship with extinction but not reward.

claim: The variations in the magnitude of the Ca+2 signal during early extinction were not due to differences in the recording location.
source: These results therefore suggest that the magnitude of the Ca+2 signal during E-Ext correlated with the level of extinction learning and the variations in the magnitude of this signal were not due to differences in the recording location.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation with reward responses.

claim: The Ca+2 signal evoked by the CS was not significantly different from the baseline during early extinction when averaged across all animals.
source: Accordingly, consistent with single unit results which showed no change in CS-evoked population activity of putative DA neurons (Figure 1J; Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), the Ca+2 signal evoked by the CS was not significantly different from the baseline during E-Ext (p = 1.0, sign-rank test) or Hab (p = 0.43, sign-rank test) when we averaged the CS responses of all animals (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of photometry data.

claim: DA neurons signal the unexpected omission of the aversive US during fear extinction and the magnitude of this DA signal predicts the strength of extinction learning.
source: Overall, these findings together with our single-unit results demonstrate that DA neurons signal the unexpected omission of the aversive US during fear extinction and that the magnitude of this DA signal predicts the strength of extinction learning.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the electrophysiology and photometry data presented.

claim: There was a high degree of overlap between Cre-dependent NpHR-eYFP expression and immunohistochemical staining against TH.
source: We observed a high degree of overlap between Cre-dependent NpHR-eYFP expression and immunohistochemical staining against TH (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C) suggesting DA neuron-selective expression.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Optical stimulation of NpHR inhibits DA neuron firing in awake DAT-cre mice.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that optical stimulation of NpHR inhibits DA neuron firing in awake DAT-cre mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Paired-NpHR group showed impaired extinction learning compared to control groups.
source: Compared to the two control groups, the Paired-NpHR group exhibited high freezing levels to the CS throughout the extinction session, suggesting impaired extinction learning (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: There was a significant main effect of group on freezing during extinction in the optogenetic inhibition experiment.
source: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of group (F2,456 = 7.03, p = 0.0052) and a significant interaction between group and trial (F48,456 = 2.19, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The Paired-NpHR group showed significantly higher freezing than control groups during late extinction.
source: Consistent with this, there was a significant difference between the Paired-NpHR group and the Paired-eYFP (p<0.001) or Unpaired-NpHR (p<0.001) controls during L-Ext (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Impaired extinction learning in the Paired-NpHR group resulted in a weaker memory for extinction when tested the next day.
source: Furthermore, impaired extinction learning resulted in a weaker memory for extinction when tested the next day (extinction recall test; two-way repeated measures ANOVA; main effect of group: F2, 456 = 7.1, p = 0.005; group × trial interaction: F48, 456 = 1.49, p = 0.02; Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis from the extinction recall test.

claim: During early extinction recall trials, the Paired-NpHR group froze significantly more compared to control groups.
source: Consistently, during the early extinction recall trials (E-Ext Rec: first 10 CSs) the Paired-NpHR group froze significantly more compared to the Paired-eYFP (p<0.001) or the Unpaired-NpHR (p<0.001) controls (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The Unpaired-NpHR group behaved comparable to the Paired-eYFP control group during both extinction and extinction recall tests.
source: In contrast to the Paired-NpHR group, the Unpaired-NpHR group behaved comparable to the Paired-eYFP control group during both extinction and extinction recall tests (Figure 5G–J) suggesting that optical inhibition of DA neurons per se did not result in a nonspecific increase in freezing levels, and that the behavioral effect was dependent on the temporally specific inhibition of DA neurons during the time of the US omission.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical comparisons.

claim: Optical inhibition of DA neurons per se did not result in a nonspecific increase in freezing levels.
source: In contrast to the Paired-NpHR group, the Unpaired-NpHR group behaved comparable to the Paired-eYFP control group during both extinction and extinction recall tests (Figure 5G–J) suggesting that optical inhibition of DA neurons per se did not result in a nonspecific increase in freezing levels, and that the behavioral effect was dependent on the temporally specific inhibition of DA neurons during the time of the US omission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between paired and unpaired inhibition groups.

claim: The behavioral effect of optogenetic inhibition was dependent on the temporally specific inhibition of DA neurons during the time of the US omission.
source: In contrast to the Paired-NpHR group, the Unpaired-NpHR group behaved comparable to the Paired-eYFP control group during both extinction and extinction recall tests (Figure 5G–J) suggesting that optical inhibition of DA neurons per se did not result in a nonspecific increase in freezing levels, and that the behavioral effect was dependent on the temporally specific inhibition of DA neurons during the time of the US omission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between paired and unpaired inhibition groups.

claim: There was no difference between groups in fear acquisition on day 1 in the optogenetic inhibition experiment.
source: Furthermore, there was no difference between the groups in their fear acquisition on day 1 (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, no main effect of group, F2,57 = 0.3, p = 0.74 or no group × trial interaction, F6,57 = 0.94, p = 0.47; Figure 5G) and all groups showed comparable levels of freezing at the start of extinction (first CS; one-way ANOVA, F2,19 = 2.06, p = 0.15; Figure 5H) before any experimental manipulation took place, ruling out the possibility that differences in the strength of fear memory on day 2 between groups might have caused the observed effect.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: All groups showed comparable levels of freezing at the start of extinction before any experimental manipulation took place.
source: Furthermore, there was no difference between the groups in their fear acquisition on day 1 (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, no main effect of group, F2,57 = 0.3, p = 0.74 or no group × trial interaction, F6,57 = 0.94, p = 0.47; Figure 5G) and all groups showed comparable levels of freezing at the start of extinction (first CS; one-way ANOVA, F2,19 = 2.06, p = 0.15; Figure 5H) before any experimental manipulation took place, ruling out the possibility that differences in the strength of fear memory on day 2 between groups might have caused the observed effect.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Freezing levels of the NpHR group at the beginning of extinction recall were comparable to freezing levels at the beginning of extinction.
source: Importantly, freezing levels of the NpHR group at the beginning of extinction recall were comparable to freezing levels at the beginning of extinction (paired t-test comparing first CS of extinction and first CS of extinction recall, t(6) = 0.56, p = 0.59), suggesting that no significant extinction learning happened in these animals.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: No significant extinction learning happened in the Paired-NpHR animals.
source: Importantly, freezing levels of the NpHR group at the beginning of extinction recall were comparable to freezing levels at the beginning of extinction (paired t-test comparing first CS of extinction and first CS of extinction recall, t(6) = 0.56, p = 0.59), suggesting that no significant extinction learning happened in these animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of change in freezing from extinction to extinction recall.

claim: The extinction rate of the Paired-NpHR group during extinction recall was comparable to the extinction rate of control groups during extinction.
source: Furthermore, we found that the extinction rate of the Paired-NpHR group during extinction recall, in the absence of optogenetic inhibition, was comparable to the extinction rate of the Paired-eYFP and Unpaired-NpHR groups during extinction (two-way repeated measures ANOVA; no main effect of group F2, 456 = 1.02, p = 0.37 and group × trial interaction: F48, 456 = 0.86, p = 0.73).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The optogenetic manipulation did not have a nonspecific long-term effect on the ability of the Paired-NpHR group to exhibit extinction learning.
source: This suggests that our manipulation did not have a nonspecific long-term effect on the ability of the Paired-NpHR group to exhibit extinction learning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the normal extinction rate during extinction recall.

claim: The optogenetic manipulation likely did not affect the strength of the fear memory.
source: These results also suggest that our optogenetic manipulation likely did not affect the strength of the fear memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparable initial freezing and normal extinction rate during recall.

claim: DA neuron activation by the unexpected omission of the US is necessary for fear extinction learning.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that DA neuron activation by the unexpected omission of the US is necessary for fear extinction learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: There was a high level of overlap between Cre-dependent ChR2-eYFP expression and immunohistochemical staining against TH.
source: There was again a high level of overlap between Cre-dependent ChR2-eYFP expression and immunohistochemical staining against TH (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C) suggesting DA neuron-selective expression of ChR2.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Optical stimulation of ChR2 induces firing of DA neurons in awake DAT-cre mice.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that optical stimulation of ChR2 induces firing of DA neurons in awake DAT-cre mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: All groups showed a gradual decrease in freezing to the CS during the extinction session in the optogenetic excitation experiment.
source: As expected, all groups showed a gradual decrease in freezing to the CS during the extinction session.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the behavioral data.

claim: In the Paired-ChR2 group, freezing decreased faster than in the control groups suggesting accelerated extinction learning.
source: However, in the Paired-ChR2 group, freezing decreased faster than in the control groups suggesting accelerated extinction learning (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: There was a significant main effect of group on freezing during extinction in the optogenetic excitation experiment.
source: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA comparing freezing levels confirmed this observation by revealing a significant main effect of group (F2,432 = 4.1, p = 0.03).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The Paired-ChR2 group exhibited significantly lower freezing compared to control groups during early extinction.
source: Comparison of freezing levels in the three groups, particularly during E-Ext, revealed a significant difference between the Paired-ChR2 group and the Paired-eYFP (p<0.05) or Unpaired-ChR2 (p<0.05) controls (Figure 6I) suggesting accelerated extinction learning.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The two control groups in the optogenetic excitation experiment behaved comparably.
source: On the other hand, the two control groups behaved comparably (p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of behavioral data.

claim: Optical excitation of DA neurons per se did not result in a nonspecific decrease in freezing levels.
source: These results suggest that optical excitation of DA neurons per se did not result in a nonspecific decrease in freezing levels and that the temporally precise excitation during the US omission is necessary for the observed behavioral effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between paired and unpaired excitation groups.

claim: Temporally precise excitation of DA neurons during the US omission is necessary for the observed behavioral effect in the optogenetic excitation experiment.
source: These results suggest that optical excitation of DA neurons per se did not result in a nonspecific decrease in freezing levels and that the temporally precise excitation during the US omission is necessary for the observed behavioral effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between paired and unpaired excitation groups.

claim: There was no difference between groups in fear acquisition on day 1 in the optogenetic excitation experiment.
source: Furthermore, there was no difference between the groups in their fear acquisition on day 1 (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, no main effect of group, F2,54 = 0.17, p = 0.84 and no group × trial interaction, F6,54 = 0.65, p = 0.68, Figure 6G) and all groups showed comparable levels of freezing during the first CS of extinction (one-way ANOVA, F2,18 = 0.81, p = 0.66, Figure 6H) before light stimulation began.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: All groups showed comparable levels of freezing during the first CS of extinction before light stimulation began in the optogenetic excitation experiment.
source: Furthermore, there was no difference between the groups in their fear acquisition on day 1 (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, no main effect of group, F2,54 = 0.17, p = 0.84 and no group × trial interaction, F6,54 = 0.65, p = 0.68, Figure 6G) and all groups showed comparable levels of freezing during the first CS of extinction (one-way ANOVA, F2,18 = 0.81, p = 0.66, Figure 6H) before light stimulation began.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Excitation of DA neurons precisely at the time of the unexpected US omission is sufficient to accelerate fear extinction learning.
source: Thus, excitation of DA neurons precisely at the time of the unexpected US omission is sufficient to accelerate fear extinction learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the optogenetic excitation experiments.

claim: Paired-ChR2 mice spent less time freezing to the CS compared to control groups during the extinction recall test.
source: Finally, Paired-ChR2 mice spent less time freezing to the CS compared to the control groups during the extinction recall test (two-way repeated measures ANOVA; main effect of group: F2,162 = 5.5, p = 0.013 and group × trial interaction: F18,162 = 2.52, p = 0.0011, Figure 6G) suggesting that the accelerated extinction learning resulted in a stronger extinction memory.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The accelerated extinction learning in the Paired-ChR2 group resulted in a stronger extinction memory.
source: Finally, Paired-ChR2 mice spent less time freezing to the CS compared to the control groups during the extinction recall test (two-way repeated measures ANOVA; main effect of group: F2,162 = 5.5, p = 0.013 and group × trial interaction: F18,162 = 2.52, p = 0.0011, Figure 6G) suggesting that the accelerated extinction learning resulted in a stronger extinction memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lower freezing during extinction recall.

claim: All groups showed high freezing to the CS during the renewal test and there was no difference in freezing levels between groups.
source: However, we found that all groups showed high freezing to the CS during the renewal test and that there was no difference in the freezing levels between the groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 3; two-way repeated measures ANOVA, no significant effect of group, F2, 72 = 0.33, p = 0.72 and group × trial interaction, F8, 72 = 0.86, p = 0.55) suggesting that all three groups showed comparable levels of fear renewal.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from the renewal test.

claim: All three groups showed comparable levels of fear renewal.
source: However, we found that all groups showed high freezing to the CS during the renewal test and that there was no difference in the freezing levels between the groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 3; two-way repeated measures ANOVA, no significant effect of group, F2, 72 = 0.33, p = 0.72 and group × trial interaction, F8, 72 = 0.86, p = 0.55) suggesting that all three groups showed comparable levels of fear renewal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the renewal test data.

claim: The low level of freezing in Paired-ChR2 group during extinction recall was not due to an effect of optogenetic manipulation on the fear memory but rather was due to enhanced extinction learning and memory formation.
source: This suggests that the low level of freezing in Paired-ChR2 group during extinction recall was not due to an affect of our optogenetic manipulation on the fear memory but rather was due to enhanced extinction learning and memory formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparable fear renewal across groups.

claim: Increasing DA neuron activity at the time of US omission is sufficient to accelerate extinction learning and strengthen extinction memory.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that increasing DA neuron activity at the time of US omission — and thus enhancing an endogenous extinction mechanism — is sufficient to accelerate extinction learning and strengthen extinction memory.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the optogenetic excitation experiments.

claim: DA neurons were activated by the omission of the aversive US during fear extinction, specifically during the beginning of extinction when the US omission is most unexpected.
source: Here we demonstrated that DA neurons were activated by the omission of the aversive US during fear extinction, specifically during the beginning of extinction when the US omission is most unexpected.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: Temporally specific optogenetic inhibition of DA neurons at the time of the US omission prevented extinction.
source: Furthermore, temporally specific optogenetic inhibition of DA neurons at the time of the US omission prevented extinction, demonstrating that this signal is necessary for normal fear extinction.
evidence: This is a summary of the optogenetic inhibition findings.

claim: Enhancing the DA signal using temporally-specific optogenetic excitation was sufficient to accelerate extinction learning.
source: Conversely, enhancing this DA signal using temporally-specific optogenetic excitation was sufficient to accelerate extinction learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the optogenetic excitation findings.

claim: DA neurons play a crucial role in signaling the unexpected omission of aversive outcomes and thereby driving fear extinction learning.
source: Together, these results identify a crucial role of DA neurons in signaling the unexpected omission of aversive outcomes and thereby driving fear extinction learning.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: DA neurons encode a reward prediction error, or the discrepancy between expected and actual rewards, which acts as a teaching signal for reinforcement learning.
source: Previous studies have shown that DA neurons encode a reward prediction error, or the discrepancy between expected and actual rewards, which acts as a teaching signal for reinforcement learning (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Eshel et al., 2015; Eshel et al., 2016; Schultz et al., 1997; Steinberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Presentation of unexpected or better than expected rewards induces increased firing in DA neurons.
source: Specifically, presentation of unexpected or better than expected rewards induces increased firing in DA neurons (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Eshel et al., 2016; Roesch et al., 2007; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: DA neurons might signal a better than expected outcome during fear extinction.
source: Our results suggest that DA neurons might also signal a better than expected outcome during fear extinction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of prediction error theory.

claim: A subpopulation of putative DA neurons in the VTA increased their firing selectively at the time of the US omission during fear extinction.
source: We found that a subpopulation of putative DA neurons in the VTA increased their firing selectively at the time of the US omission during fear extinction.
evidence: This is a summary of the electrophysiology findings.

claim: US omission-responsive firing was observed specifically during the early trials of extinction when the absence of the US was unexpected.
source: This US omission-responsive firing was observed specifically during the early trials of extinction when the absence of the US was unexpected, and was significantly reduced during the late stages of extinction when the US omission was no longer unexpected and animals showed significant extinction of fear responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the temporal dynamics of the DA response.

claim: US omission responses were not observed in putative non-DA neurons.
source: Importantly, these responses were not observed in putative non-DA neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the cell-type specificity of the response.

claim: DA neurons encode a prediction error-like signal during fear extinction learning.
source: This suggests that DA neurons encode a prediction error-like signal during fear extinction learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: DA neurons not only encode reward prediction errors but also signal prediction errors to gate fear learning.
source: Recent studies have shown that DA neurons not only encode reward prediction errors but also signal prediction errors to gate fear learning (Groessl et al., 2018) and to drive threat avoidance (Menegas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Omission of aversive stimuli during fear extinction in fruit flies is encoded by the DA system that mediates reward, but not aversive, learning.
source: Interestingly, omission of aversive stimuli during fear extinction in fruit flies is encoded by the DA system that mediates reward, but not aversive, learning (Felsenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to research in fruit flies.

claim: Previous studies using partial reinforcement paradigms have shown that DA neurons exhibit increased firing to the unexpected omission of aversive stimuli.
source: Consistent with our results, previous studies using partial reinforcement paradigms have shown that DA neurons exhibit increased firing to the unexpected omission of aversive stimuli (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Matsumoto et al., 2016; but see Tian and Uchida, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Responses to aversive US omission in previous studies were much smaller compared to what was observed in this study.
source: However, responses to aversive US omission in these studies were much smaller compared to what we observed.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: The valence of the testing context influences DA neuron responses to the omission of the aversive US.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that the valence of the testing context influences DA neuron responses to the omission of the aversive US. Matsumoto and colleagues (2016) found a significant increase in DA neuron responses to the omission of aversive airpuff in a low reward, but not high reward, context.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: DA neurons signal better than expected outcomes more generally, such as the omission of an aversive event.
source: Overall, our findings suggest that DA neurons not only signal better than expected rewards (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Eshel et al., 2016; Roesch et al., 2007; Schultz et al., 1997) but also better than expected outcomes more generally, such as the omission of an aversive event.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and comparison with previous literature.

claim: Detecting the discrepancy between expected and actual outcomes is critical for new learning.
source: Detecting the discrepancy between expected and actual outcomes is critical for new learning (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972).
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of learning theory supported by citation.

claim: During fear extinction, the omission of the aversive US is an unexpected outcome which initiates new learning about the CS.
source: During fear extinction, the omission of the aversive US is an unexpected outcome which initiates new learning about the CS, specifically that it no longer predicts danger.
evidence: This is an application of learning theory principles to fear extinction.

claim: How extinction learning is initiated at the neuronal level has remained unknown.
source: However, how this learning is initiated at the neuronal level has remained unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The DA signal during the omission of the aversive US drives normal fear extinction learning.
source: Here, by using bidirectional optogenetic manipulations, we demonstrated that the DA signal during the omission of the aversive US drives normal fear extinction learning: inhibiting this DA signal prevented, while enhancing it accelerated, normal extinction learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the causal optogenetic findings.

claim: The results are consistent with previous findings establishing the causal role of DA neurons in reinforcement learning.
source: Our results are consistent with previous findings establishing the causal role of DA neurons in reinforcement learning (Chang et al., 2016; Steinberg et al., 2013; Tsai et al., 2009) and further extend their role to safety learning.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature supported by citations.

claim: A recent study inhibited VTA DA neurons during US omission in rats and found reduced fear extinction learning.
source: Consistent with our findings, a recent study inhibited VTA DA neurons during US omission in rats and also found reduced fear extinction learning (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Enhancement of DA signaling by L-DOPA administration during extinction was sufficient to initiate fear extinction learning in a mouse model of impaired extinction learning.
source: Consistent with our results, it has been shown that enhancement of DA signaling by L-DOPA administration during extinction was sufficient to initiate fear extinction learning in a mouse model of impaired extinction learning (Whittle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Enhancement of DA signaling during extinction could be a potential strategy for the treatment of anxiety disorders.
source: Our results therefore suggest that enhancement of DA signaling during extinction could be a potential strategy for the treatment of anxiety disorders.
evidence: This is a speculation about clinical implications based on the experimental findings.

claim: Fear extinction is mediated by a network of brain structures consisting mainly of the amygdala and the infra-limbic subregion of the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: Fear extinction is mediated by a network of brain structures consisting mainly of the amygdala and the infra-limbic (IL) subregion of the medial prefrontal cortex (Duvarci and Pare, 2014; Maren et al., 2013; Pape and Pare, 2010; Sotres-Bayon and Quirk, 2010; Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neuronal activation in the amygdala and IL occurs during the CS and later than the DA signal observed in this study.
source: Although neuronal activation has been observed in these structures during different stages of fear extinction, they occur during the CS and later than the DA signal we observed in our study.
evidence: This is a comparison of the timing of responses in different brain regions.

claim: In the basolateral amygdala, a subpopulation of neurons termed 'extinction neurons' increases their firing to the CS during extinction learning.
source: In the basolateral amygdala, a subpopulation of neurons termed 'extinction neurons' increases their firing to the CS during extinction learning (Amano et al., 2011; Herry et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Extinction neurons in the amygdala become CS responsive late in the extinction session right before the animals show a decrease in fear responses.
source: However, these neurons become CS responsive late in the extinction session right before the animals show a decrease in fear responses (Herry et al., 2008) suggesting that these neurons likely mediate inhibition of fear responses.
evidence: This is supported by citation and includes an inference about function.

claim: In the IL, increased firing to the CS is observed during extinction recall.
source: In the IL, a structure necessary for consolidation of extinction memories (Sotres-Bayon and Quirk, 2010), increased firing to the CS is observed during extinction recall (Milad and Quirk, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The DA signal occurs at the early trials of the extinction session, supporting the conclusion that this signal initiates extinction learning.
source: In contrast, the DA signal that we demonstrated in our study occurs at the early trials of the extinction session, supporting our conclusion that this signal initiates extinction learning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of the DA signal compared to other brain regions.

claim: Plasticity in the amygdala and IL underlie acquisition and consolidation of fear extinction memories.
source: Plasticity in the amygdala and IL underlie acquisition and consolidation of fear extinction memories (Duvarci and Pare, 2014; Maren et al., 2013; Pape and Pare, 2010; Sotres-Bayon and Quirk, 2010; Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: DA signaling in the amygdala and IL has been shown to play an important role in fear extinction.
source: Furthermore, DA signaling in the amygdala and IL has been shown to play an important role in fear extinction (Abraham et al., 2014; Haaker et al., 2013; Hikind and Maroun, 2008; Mueller et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2017; Whittle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of DA neurons during US omission prevents extinction-related plasticity in the amygdala and IL.
source: Interestingly, optogenetic inhibition of DA neurons during US omission has been found to prevent extinction-related plasticity in the amygdala and IL (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: It is unclear how the DA signal induces plasticity in the amygdala and IL to underlie extinction memory.
source: However, it is unclear how this DA signal induces plasticity in the amygdala and IL to underlie extinction memory.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Midbrain DA neurons form functionally distinct and mostly non-overlapping subpopulations based on their projection targets.
source: Recent studies have shown that midbrain DA neurons form functionally distinct and mostly non-overlapping subpopulations based on their projection targets (Beier et al., 2015; Lammel et al., 2008; Lammel et al., 2011; Lerner et al., 2015; Lynd-Balta and Haber, 1994; Menegas et al., 2015; Menegas et al., 2017; Parker et al., 2016; Roeper, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: One possible candidate for the DA neurons that respond to US omission is the subpopulation projecting to the NAc.
source: One possible candidate is the subpopulation projecting to the NAc.
evidence: This is speculation about which DA neuron subpopulation is involved.

claim: An increase in DA release around the time of the CS offset during fear extinction has been observed in the NAc.
source: Supporting this possibility, an increase in DA release around the time of the CS offset during fear extinction has been observed in the NAc (Badrinarayan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The increase in DA release in the NAc was observed only during the early trials of extinction.
source: In particular, this was observed only during the early trials of extinction, consistent with our results.
evidence: This is supported by citation and comparison with the current findings.

claim: DA signaling in the NAc has been shown to be important for relief learning.
source: DA signaling in the NAc has also been shown to be important for relief learning (Mayer et al., 2018) and avoidance behavior (Gentry et al., 2016; Oleson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of DA receptors in the NAc impairs fear extinction learning.
source: Notably, pharmacological blockade of DA receptors in the NAc have been found to impair fear extinction learning (Holtzman-Assif et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Fear extinction learning in humans is accompanied by a prediction error-like activation in the ventral striatum.
source: Furthermore, we have observed that fear extinction learning in humans is accompanied by a prediction error-like activation in the ventral striatum (Raczka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: Inhibition of DA terminals in NAc or DA neurons projecting to the medial shell of NAc during US omission did not affect fear extinction learning.
source: However, at odds with these findings, inhibition of DA terminals in NAc or DA neurons projecting to the medial shell of NAc during US omission did not affect fear extinction learning, although it did impair consolidation of extinction memory, in a recent study (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: A small subpopulation of DA neurons mediates the DA signal that drives extinction learning.
source: Our single unit results demonstrate that a small subpopulation of DA neurons mediate this DA signal to drive extinction learning.
evidence: This is based on the single-unit recording data showing only 25% of DA neurons respond.

claim: Identifying which projection-defined subpopulation of DA neurons signals the omission of the US to initiate fear extinction learning will be an important question for future research.
source: Identifying which projection-defined subpopulation of DA neurons signals the omission of the US to initiate fear extinction learning will be an important question for future research.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: This study identifies a prediction error-like signal encoded by DA neurons that is necessary to initiate fear extinction learning.
source: In conclusion, our study identifies a prediction error-like signal encoded by DA neurons that is necessary to initiate fear extinction learning.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Enhancing the DA signal is sufficient to accelerate extinction learning and strengthen extinction memory consolidation.
source: Furthermore, we found that enhancing this DA signal is sufficient to accelerate extinction learning and strengthen extinction memory consolidation.
evidence: This is a summary of the optogenetic excitation findings.

claim: Deficits in fear extinction learning are thought to underlie anxiety disorders.
source: Deficits in fear extinction learning are thought to underlie anxiety disorders (Craske et al., 2017; Graham and Milad, 2011; Mahan and Ressler, 2012; Milad and Quirk, 2012; Pitman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: This study has therapeutic implications for anxiety disorders by identifying DA neuron activity as a potential target for novel treatments.
source: Our study therefore has therapeutic implications for anxiety disorders by identifying DA neuron activity as a potential target for novel treatments.
evidence: This is a speculation about clinical implications based on the experimental findings.

claim: Male C57BL/6N mice aged 3 months were used in the in vivo electrophysiology experiment.
source: Male C57BL/6N mice (Charles River), aged 3 months at the start of experiments, were used in the in vivo electrophysiology experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Male heterozygous DAT-Cre mice aged 3–6 months were used in the photometry and optogenetics experiments.
source: Male heterozygous DAT-Cre mice (Zhuang et al., 2005; backcrossed with C57BL/6N) aged 3–6 months at the start of experiments were used in the photometry and optogenetics experiments.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Neurons whose baseline firing rate were below 10 Hz and exhibited long duration action potentials (peak-to-peak duration >450 µs) were classified as putative DA neurons.
source: We therefore classified neurons whose baseline firing rate (measured in the home cage) were below 10 Hz and exhibited long duration action potentials (peak-to-peak duration >450 µs) as putative DA neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a description of the classification criteria used in the analysis.

claim: 97.1% of GFP+ neurons in the gCaMP6 group were TH+.
source: Both groups showed similarly high levels of DA specificity (gCaMP6: 97.1%; GFP: 95.8%).
evidence: This is supported by histological quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 95.8% of GFP+ neurons in the GFP control group were TH+.
source: Both groups showed similarly high levels of DA specificity (gCaMP6: 97.1%; GFP: 95.8%).
evidence: This is supported by histological quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 95.3% of eYFP+ neurons in the NpHR-eYFP group were TH+.
source: Both groups showed similarly high levels of specificity for DA neurons (NpHR-eYFP: 95.3%; eYFP: 95%).
evidence: This is supported by histological quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 95% of eYFP+ neurons in the eYFP control group were TH+.
source: Both groups showed similarly high levels of specificity for DA neurons (NpHR-eYFP: 95.3%; eYFP: 95%).
evidence: This is supported by histological quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 95.9% of eYFP+ neurons in the ChR2-eYFP group were TH+.
source: Both groups showed similarly high levels of specificity for DA neurons (ChR2-eYFP: 95.9%; eYFP: 95.1%).
evidence: This is supported by histological quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 95.1% of eYFP+ neurons in the eYFP control group were TH+.
source: Both groups showed similarly high levels of specificity for DA neurons (ChR2-eYFP: 95.9%; eYFP: 95.1%).
evidence: This is supported by histological quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.
